Damminga, Helle-Brit Fiebrich, Wouter H. de Vos tot Nederveen Cappel, Henderik L. van Westreenen Introduction After curative surgery for colorectal cancer (CRC), patients undergo surveillance because of the risk of recurrence; however, only a subset develops recurrence amenable to further curative-intent treatment. The primary aim of follow‑up is to identify patients with potentially curable recurrence. Materials and methods A retrospective analysis was performed of stage I–IV CRC patients who underwent curative-intent treatment and entered postoperative surveillance at Isala between 2014 and 2018. Follow‑up was conducted according to Dutch guideline‑based protocols for 60 months. Patients were categorized as having no recurrence, a potentially curable recurrence, or a non-curable recurrence. Prognostic factors at start of follow-up for potentially curable recurrence were assessed using competing‑risk Cox regression, with non-curable recurrence and death as competing events. For patients with recurrence, mode and time of detection were evaluated. Results During a median follow-up of 60 months, recurrence occurred in 22.4% of 1118 patients. The cumulative incidence function (CIF) of a potentially curable recurrence was 8.0%. Independent variables associated with a potentially curable recurrence were age HR 0.97 (95% CI 0.96–0.99), minor postoperative complications HR 1.78 (95% CI 1.16–2.72), stage III CRC HR2.76 (95% CI 1.19–6.38) and stage IV CRC HR 11.02 (95% CI 4.44–27.37). Among patients with a recurrence, CEA ≥ 5 ng/mL was present in 63% of all recurrences, but less often in the potentially curable group (57% vs. 69%, p = 0.057). Median time to detection of a potentially curable recurrence was 16 months (IQR 20). The overall number needed to follow-up (NNFU) to detect one potentially curable recurrence was 9.8, with the lowest NNFU observed in stage IV CRC (2.3) and in rectal cancer (6.9). Conclusion Standard follow-up enabled the detection of potentially curable recurrence in 8% of CRC patients. The substantial variation in NNFU across subgroups and the limited sensitivity of CEA underscore the need for more personalized, risk‑adapted surveillance strategies.
n9ddbd15c99b6: Background Public health nurses play a pivotal role in primary public health services, yet China lacks a systematic, context-specific competency framework to support workforce development. This study aimed to develop a competency framework for public health nurses in China to guide capacity-building initiatives. Methods A preliminary competency framework was constructed based on a literature review, job analysis, and semi-structured interviews with 22 frontline practitioners and comprised six domains, 16 subdomains, and 52 competencies. A two-round Delphi survey was then conducted with 21 experts from multiple regions with expertise in community nursing, public health, primary care medicine, and nursing education and related specialties. Consensus was defined as a mean importance rating ≥4.0 (5-point Likert scale) and a coefficient of variation ≤0.25. The Delphi consultation process was characterized by expert engagement, the expert authority coefficient, and the coordination of expert opinions. Finally, the Analytic Hierarchy Process was applied to determine the relative weights of the agreed-upon items at each level. Results Across the two Delphi rounds, the response rates were 95.45% and 100%, the expert authority coefficient was 0.90, and Kendall’s coefficients of concordance were 0.156 and 0.171, respectively (both P < 0.001). The final competency framework comprised six domains, 16 subdomains, and 46 competencies. All Analytic Hierarchy Process judgment matrices showed acceptable consistency (CR < 0.10). Health education and health promotion was assigned the highest weight (0.280) among the domains. Conclusion The resulting competency framework demonstrates methodological rigor, a comprehensive structure, and contextual relevance. It provides theoretical and practical implications for competency-based education, workforce development, and the professionalization of public health nursing in China.
n11068f193537: by Md. Helal Uddin, Pronesh Dutta, Monjurul Islam, Md. Kaisar Rahman, Shariful Islam, Md. Rezaul Karim, Farhana Rahman, Jade K. Forwood, Sharmin Chowdhury, Jonathan H. Epstein, Mohammed Abdus Samad, Ariful Islam Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a growing global threat to both animal and human health, underscoring the importance of AMR surveillance across all sectors of the One Health triad, including wildlife. Fruit bats in Bangladesh frequently inhabit areas in close proximity to human settlements and livestock facilities, creating ecological conditions that facilitate the co-occurrence of AMR bacteria through direct contact or shared contaminated environments. A cross-sectional study was conducted to determine the prevalence of Salmonella spp. isolation and the proportion of antimicrobial-resistant isolates among confirmed positives, characterize resistance patterns across multiple antimicrobial classes, and identify associated risk factors in fruit bat populations and environmental water sources in Bangladesh. We collected 369 fecal samples from the roosts of two bat species, Pteropus medius and Rousettus leschenaultii, along with 22 water samples from water bodies utilized by humans, livestock, and bats. Salmonella spp. isolates were identified using selective agar culture, followed by biochemical testing and confirmation via polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Confirmed isolates underwent antimicrobial susceptibility testing via the Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion method against 12 antimicrobials. The prevalence of AMR Salmonella spp. was 7.9% (95% CI: 5.3–11.1%) in bat’s roost fecal samples and 31.8% (95% CI: 13.9–54.9%) in environmental water samples. Bat-derived isolates showed high resistance to tetracycline (93%), nalidixic acid (86%), sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim (80%), and azithromycin (76%). Among the identified AMR isolates, 28 (96.5%) met the criteria for multidrug resistance (MDR), defined as resistance to three or more antimicrobial classes. Water-derived isolates also demonstrated high resistance, particularly to tetracycline (86%), amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (75%), azithromycin (73%), ceftriaxone (72%), and ciprofloxacin (71%). Multivariable logistic regression analysis revealed that the odds ratio (OR) of detection of MDR Salmonella spp. in fruit bats was 5.1 times higher during the summer season compared to winter. These findings highlight the evidence of MDR Salmonella spp. in fruit bats and shared environmental water sources in Bangladesh. The co-occurrence of resistant isolates across wildlife and environmental samples highlights the need for integrated AMR surveillance encompassing wildlife reservoirs and shared ecological interfaces. Strengthened antimicrobial stewardship, improved wastewater management, and coordinated One Health surveillance strategies are essential to mitigate the risk of zoonotic spillover and reduce further ecological overlap of MDR bacteria at the wildlife–livestock–human interface in Bangladesh and the broader South Asian region.
nb8913d7b9cd6: Background Insomnia and poor sleep are highly prevalent among university students and are linked to impaired mental and physical health, reduced cognitive functioning, and lower academic performance. Existing interventions for insomnia include cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), mindfulness, and sleep hygiene. CBT-I is widely recognised as effective but remains difficult to access for the general population and lack scalability, long-term follow-up, and feasibility in non-clinical settings. Pragmatic, group-based approaches that can be delivered within the university and are tailored to help students develop self-endorsed routines and competencies for better sleep, creating sustainable changes that extend beyond the program period, is needed. Methods This study is a pragmatic, two-arm randomised controlled trial evaluating the effectiveness of a group-based sleep program for university students with insomnia symptoms. A total of 118 full-time students aged 18–30 meeting diagnostic criteria for chronic insomnia disorder will be randomized (1:1) to either the intervention or a wait-list control group. The intervention comprises 12 weekly 90-minute group sessions followed by nine monthly follow-up meetings, facilitated by trained coaches. The program integrates core elements of CBT-I with motivational and coping strategies, delivered in an interactive and peer-supported format. The primary outcome is change in insomnia severity measured by the Bergen Insomnia Scale. Secondary outcomes include subjective and objective sleep measures, mental health, cognitive performance, academic attainment, health behaviours, physical fitness, and biological markers. Assessments will be conducted at baseline, post-program (12 weeks), and 12 months. A mixed methods process evaluation will assess fidelity, acceptability, mechanisms of impact, and contextual influences. Discussion This trial will be among the first pragmatic evaluations of a structured, group-based sleep intervention tailored to university students with insomnia. Key strengths include the randomised controlled design, comprehensive outcome assessment, 12-month follow-up, and embedded process evaluation. If effective, the program could provide a feasible, scalable, and cost-effective model to improve sleep and therein health, and academic performance in young adults in higher education.
nfa442d424008: Electronic health record-based oncology studies depend on computable case definitions, but different operational definitions may identify different patient populations and change downstream estimates. This retrospective benchmarking cohort study evaluated three definitions of incident invasive breast cancer in the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network: at least one malignant breast cancer diagnosis code (Dx1), a repeated diagnosis-code definition within 90 days (Dx2), and a diagnosis code plus breast cancer-directed treatment evidence (DxTx). Female patients aged 20 years or older were identified after a 12-month washout period and exclusion of patients with carcinoma in situ only. Pairwise one-to-one propensity-score matching was performed using 13 baseline covariates. Outcomes were all-cause mortality and time to the first emergency department visits, assessed from day 180 after the index date to 1, 3, and 5 years after the original index date. Appendicitis and femoral neck fracture were included as negative-control outcomes. Dx1, Dx2, and DxTx identified 1,450,233, 678,739, and 578,576 patients, respectively. After matching, more restrictive definitions were consistently associated with higher hazards of mortality and emergency department visits. For mortality, hazard ratios ranged from 1.26 to 1.32 for DxTx versus Dx1, 1.13 to 1.14 for Dx2 versus Dx1, and 1.13 to 1.17 for DxTx versus Dx2 across assessment windows. Emergency department visit estimates showed a similar but attenuating pattern. These associations should be interpreted as differences between phenotype-defined populations arising from selection and ascertainment mechanisms rather than as treatment effects. Negative-control outcomes were generally close to the null; small appendicitis associations observed in comparisons involving Dx1 did not remain statistically significant after correction for multiple testing. These findings indicate that plausible electronic health record-based breast cancer definitions are not analytically interchangeable. Phenotype specification should therefore be treated as a core analytic decision and evaluated through transparent reporting and sensitivity analyses.
nc4872082183e: by Cornelia Herbert Academic performance involves achieving one’s goals and reaching one’s full potential while staying mentally, emotionally, and physically well. This can be challenging across all career paths. This article presents results from a new survey examining key psychological factors and how early-career researchers evaluate them in relation to their scientific performance and health as they pursue their career goals. A total of 475 participants (e.g., in Germany, Switzerland, or Austria) evaluated psychological factors that, according to previous research and psychological theories, influence academic success. The evaluations included participants’ assessments of their self-competence, motivation, and work effort; achievement emotions (including negative and positive experiences that influence well-being); perceptions of supervision; and views on reasons for staying or leaving academia. Gender differences and differences between PhDs and postdocs were also analyzed. Overall, PhD students and postdocs felt confident in and satisfied with their academic performance. They evaluated their competencies, effort, and motivation as key to achieving their career goals. Satisfaction, effort, and self-efficacy showed no gender differences, but women reported higher levels of worry and negative emotions, particularly among postdocs. Challenges such as time and financial constraints, as well as the benefits of working outside academia, influenced self-perceptions of career decisions. Most participants reported regular supervision; a few had experience with or were participating in early-career initiatives. The study emphasizes the need to consider young scientists’ beliefs, feelings, and expectations about their academic performance, achievement, and health when developing early-career strategies to reduce perceived barriers and reflect career decisions. The current approach and results are discussed in relation to previous studies, the observed challenges, and the gaps this research addresses.
n0f9803e25bd4: Remote sensing images usually exhibits densely distributed targets and scale disparities. In such scenarios, it is still challenging to preserve high detection precision while controlling costs and inference latency. To address this issue, we propose GFLNet, a lightweight single-stage detector, which is based on collaborative feature modeling and knowledge-guided compression. Specifically, Ghost-Shuffle dual fusion convolution (GSD-Fuse) is designed to achieve efficient spatial-channel interaction while reducing computational cost; an adaptive receptive-field selection module inspired by LSKNet is introduced into the deeper backbone and neck stages to adaptively adjust contextual responses for small-object and multi-scale detection; finally, LB-Compress combines layer-adaptive magnitude pruning with Bidirectional Cross-task Knowledge Distillation (BCKD) to form a compact network suitable for practical deployment. Evaluated on the DIOR and UCAS-AOD datasets, GFLNet improves mAP@0.5 over the baseline by 3.9% and 3.4%, respectively. Moreover, the model contains only 2.35M parameters, with a calculation of 5.6 GFLOPs, and an inference speed of 261 FPS on the GPU, thereby delivering a favorable accuracy-efficiency synergy.
nec2d32481229: The increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance has underscored the need for novel antimicrobial agents. Members of the genus Burkholderia produce a diverse array of antimicrobial metabolites; however, the biosynthetic potential of Burkholderia glumae, a plant pathogen, remains relatively underexplored. In this study, we investigated the biosynthetic potential, antibacterial activity, and metabolomic profiles of 16 B. glumae isolates collected from Thailand. Genome mining using antiSMASH and DeepBGC identified 14–17 and 40–51 biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) per genome, respectively. Multiple conserved BGC classes were detected across all isolates, including terpene-, polyketide-, and nonribosomal peptide-associated clusters. DeepBGC further predicted that 22–32 BGCs per isolate were associated with antibacterial activity. Phenotypic screening using soft-agar overlay assays on LB agar demonstrated that all 16 isolates displayed antibacterial activity against clinically important bacterial pathogens, including Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli, and Staphylococcus aureus. Four isolates exhibiting the strongest antibacterial activity were selected for further metabolomic analysis. Untargeted LC–MS/MS profiling of extracts from inoculated and uninoculated LB agar plates identified 68 putatively annotated antimicrobial-related metabolites shared among all four isolates and significantly enriched relative to the uninoculated controls (fold change > 2, p B. glumae isolates from Thailand possess diverse biosynthetic capabilities and antibacterial activity against clinically important bacterial pathogens, highlight the potential of these isolates as a source of bioactive metabolites for future efforts in antimicrobial agent discovery.
nb275d3bd119e: Diabetes mellitus and chronic inflammation are global health issues, exacerbated by the incomplete control of metabolic-inflammatory pathways and the adverse effects of long-term pharmacotherapy. The development of multifunctional therapeutic nanomaterials via green nanotechnology has recently garnered attention. In this study, we synthesized copper-based nanoparticles (Cu NPs) using Salvia hispanica (chia) seed-derived polysaccharides and characterized their in vitro anti-inflammatory and antidiabetic activities, as well as in vivo antidiabetic effects in an alloxan-induced diabetic mouse model. Successful formation of polysaccharide-based Cu NPs was confirmed using UV-Visible, FTIR, XRD, and SEM analyses. Hemocompatibility assessment showed concentration-dependent hemolysis by Cu NPs (0.92 ± 0.06%, 5.71 ± 0.44%, and 8.42 ± 0.63% at the respective tested concentrations), indicating reduced hemocompatibility at higher concentrations. In the HRBC membrane stabilization assay, Cu NPs exhibited dose-dependent inhibition of hemolysis (45.83 ± 1.7% to 70.59 ± 2.1%), while heat hemolysis was reduced by 72.91 ± 1.5% at 1000 µg/mL. Enzyme inhibition studies showed significant inhibition of α-amylase (58.45 ± 0.7% to 87.20 ± 2.1%) and α-glucosidase (83.87 ± 1.6% at 1000 µg/mL) compared to acarbose. Glucose uptake in yeast cells increased to 59.87 ± 0.3% at 1000 µg/mL. In alloxan-induced diabetic mice, Cu NPs (150 mg/kg) reduced fasting blood glucose from 287 ± 4.2 to 131 ± 7.02 mg/dL over 30 days and improved lipid profiles (e.g., decreased total cholesterol to 85 ± 1.3 mg/dL and increased HDL to 39.8 ± 1.2 mg/dL). Histopathological analyses showed restoration of pancreatic and hepatic architecture. Collectively, chia seed polysaccharide-mediated copper-based nanoparticles exhibited anti-hyperglycemic, anti-inflammatory, and lipid-modulating activities under the investigated experimental conditions, supporting their further evaluation for diabetes-related applications.
n4e726d99b310: Foundational to an estuarine ecosystem is the composition of its sediments, with benthic foraminifera serving as a key component. While it is common to find intact and deformed tests, foraminiferal organic linings (FOLs; foraminifera whose tests dissolved) are not always present in sediment samples. Identifying where FOLs are preserved is a necessary first step towards determining what promotes their development and burial. Here we document the prevalence of globothalamean FOLs in the Hudson River Estuary (HRE) at the Pier in Piermont, New York, USA. We also identified six agglutinated foraminifera species and successfully imaged foraminifera that were collected while in the process of losing their tests. There are a multitude of factors that can lead to test dissolution with FOL preservation, but most are related to suboptimal growth conditions. While the HRE has a history of sediment pollution, studies utilizing foraminifera or FOLs to study the modern benthic environment are not common. Our study provides some of the first evidence for FOLs preserved in the HRE. This exploratory work is a critical step towards utilizing foraminifera as a proxy for benthic conditions, with specific recommendations for future FOL sampling to monitor sediment conditions in the HRE.
n07d504618ba5: L-lysine stands out as a commercially important amino acid vital for maintaining balanced nutrition, immune function and healthy development in humans and animals. As global demand for lysine continues to rise each year, large-scale production is required to keep pace with this growing need. In the present study, L-lysine production was accomplished through a fermentation process utilizing isolated bacterial strains from soil. After conducting primary screening, Bacillus megaterium NTJT4 was identified as the highest lysine producer. Various fermentation parameters including fermentation time, pH, temperature, different carbon and nitrogen sources, glucose levels, ammonium sulfate concentration, growth stimulators, and vitamin concentrations were evaluated to optimize lysine production. The study found that the optimal conditions for lysine production were 72 hours, pH 7.0, and 37 °C. The effect of different carbon and nitrogen sources showed that 8% glucose and 1% ammonium sulfate resulted in increased lysine production (4.86 ± 0.20 mg/mL and 3.95 ± 0.14 mg/mL respectively). Media with combination of peptone and yeast extract as growth stimulators showed increased lysine yield (4.86 ± 0.31 mg/mL) and addition of 100 µg/mL thiamine-HCL as a source of vitamin resulted in increased lysine yield (5.37 ± 0.16 mg/mL). Amberlite IR‑120–based ion‑exchange chromatography achieved 100.0% purity and 58.0% recovery of lysine. The purified lysine concentration reached 13.44 mg/mL with a purification fold of 3.85. These results indicate that the newly isolated Bacillus megaterium NTJT4 possesses considerable potential for diverse biotechnological and industrial applications, particularly in microbial amino acid production.
n668744bf0933: Climbing plants rely on exploratory movements to locate and reach supports in the environment. Circumnutation is central to this exploratory behavior, yet little is known about the physiological signaling dynamics that accompany this movement. Here we show that the presence or absence of a climbing support is associated with distinct volatile organic compounds (VOCs) intensity profiles in Pisum sativum plants. Using temporal analyses aligned with circumnutation cycles, we detected distinct VOCs patterns in plants growing with or without a potential support in the surrounding environment, even before physical contact occurs. Overall VOCs intensity and the coupling between VOCs signals and circumnutation movement descriptors were higher when supports were absent. This pattern suggests that support-seeking movements are associated with metabolic changes that are in line with early physiological adjustment associated with the environmental context. Our findings identify a previously undescribed association between VOCs dynamics and circumnutation modulation during support searching in climbing plants.
ne2c23230aa60: Introduction Concept analysis is widely used in nursing and health-related disciplines to clarify ambiguous constructs, refine disciplinary language and support theory development, instrument construction, education and practice. However, concept analysis is methodologically plural rather than a single uniform method. Different approaches vary in their assumptions, data sources, analytic steps and expected outputs. Aims This scoping review will identify methodological lineages of concept analysis and map reporting elements across nursing and health-related disciplines. It will examine both the cross-lineage applicability and the empirical distribution of candidate reporting elements. Methods The review will follow Joanna Briggs Institute guidance for scoping reviews and will be reported according to the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews. Ten English- and Chinese-language databases will be searched from inception to the final search date, supplemented by targeted citation searching for foundational methodological sources. Two reviewers will independently screen records after calibration on a purposively enriched set of 25 records containing likely inclusions, likely exclusions and borderline records. Formal screening will begin after both overall raw agreement and positive agreement for the include/uncertain decision reach at least 75%; raw agreement and Cohen’s kappa will be reported before consensus. Data will be charted using a piloted form and synthesised descriptively through deductive-inductive framework analysis. Reporting elements will be mapped by both methodological applicability and empirical distribution. Conclusion The review will provide a structured account of concept analysis methods and reporting elements. It represents an evidence-mapping and candidate-item generation stage and will not itself produce a formal reporting guideline. The protocol is registered on the Open Science Framework: https://osf.io/xru7f.
n960d75c8831c: Introduction Pre-eclampsia, a high-risk pregnancy complication, poses significant threats to maternal and fetal health. Globally, little is known about how women navigate a pre-eclampsia diagnosis or their perceptions of the pathology, unpredictable course, and treatment. Guided by the Health Belief model, this study explores pregnant women’s beliefs about pre-eclampsia in Ghana’s most populous region. Materials and methods A qualitative descriptive study was conducted at a district hospital in the Ashanti Region of Ghana to explore pregnant women’s narratives of their health beliefs and perceptions regarding pre-eclampsia. Sixteen participants were purposively selected, and one-on-one semi-structured interviews were conducted in October 2021. Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis. Categories were developed inductively from participants’ accounts and subsequently interpreted in relation to the constructs of the Health Belief Model. Results Pregnant women’s risk perceptions of pre-eclampsia varied, with some not perceiving personal risk, while a few felt vulnerable based on community experiences and observations of other women. Pre-eclampsia was widely regarded as a serious condition, with many expressing fears of adverse maternal and fetal outcomes. Participants recognized the benefits of antenatal care and lifestyle modifications in reducing risk and empowering care-seeking, while previous experiences with pre-eclampsia and guidance from health providers served as key cues to action. However, several barriers to care were identified, including financial constraints, mistrust of the health system, and inadequate communication from health providers. Conclusion This study highlights the need for context-specific approaches to address health beliefs related to pre-eclampsia. Strengthening maternal health literacy, effective risk communication, and respectful care can improve early recognition, care-seeking, and outcomes for pre-eclampsia.
n8b5e611c37b2: Background Systemic inflammation is associated with the prognosis of clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). The C-reactive protein-to-lymphocyte ratio (CLR) combines systemic inflammation and host immune status. However, its prognostic value in non-metastatic ccRCC remains unclear. This study evaluated the association between preoperative CLR and survival outcomes in patients with non-metastatic ccRCC. Methods We retrospectively included 414 patients with non-metastatic ccRCC who underwent partial or radical nephrectomy. The primary Cox analyses treated ln(CLR) as a continuous variable and assessed overall survival (OS) and the cause-specific hazard of ccRCC-related death. Sensitivity analyses included expanded adjustment and time-varying effects. Cut-off-based analyses were exploratory. Time-dependent receiver operating characteristic curves were used to compare CLR with other inflammatory markers. Incremental discrimination and calibration were assessed using bootstrap internal validation. Results After adjustment for age, Fuhrman grade, and T stage, ln(CLR) remained independently associated with OS (HR = 1.589, 95% CI 1.257–2.009; P P < 0.001). The associations persisted in sensitivity analyses addressing additional pathological factors and time-varying effects. The 3- and 5-year AUCs of CLR for OS were 0.810 and 0.776, respectively. No statistically significant AUC differences were detected between CLR and CRP, NLR, or CAR. Adding CLR increased the apparent C-index from 0.843 to 0.885. After bootstrap optimism correction, the C-indices were 0.832 and 0.873, respectively (ΔC-index = 0.041). Calibration was assessed at 3 and 5 years. Conclusions Preoperative CLR was independently associated with OS and the cause-specific hazard of ccRCC-related death in this single-center cohort. Adding CLR improved discrimination after internal validation, but its superiority over other inflammatory markers and clinical utility remain unestablished. Independent multicenter validation is needed.
n6a9db44893b4: Background Employed family caregivers of people with dementia face competing work and caregiving demands that can negatively affect well-being across both domains. The Work–Home Resources model proposes that demands and resources influence cross-domain functioning through changes in personal resources. Psychological flexibility (PF), the ability to remain open to difficult experiences while acting in line with personal values, may represent a dynamic personal resource in this process. However, its real-time role in the daily work–caregiving interface remains largely unknown. Objective This protocol describes the DAILY-FLEX study, which aims to investigate momentary and daily bidirectional spillover between work and caregiving demands/resources and domain-specific well-being, and to examine whether PF mediates these associations. Methods This observational intensive longitudinal study uses Experience Sampling Methodology combined with baseline assessment. A minimum of 30 employed family caregivers of people with dementia will be recruited in the Netherlands through memory clinics, caregiver networks, and community outreach. Participants will complete a baseline questionnaire followed by a 14-day ESM protocol consisting of eight semi-random momentary assessments and one evening questionnaire per day using the m-Path smartphone application. Momentary assessments capture contextual demands and resources, PF, caregiving-related affect, and work engagement. Evening questionnaires assess daily work and caregiving demands/resources, PF, general well-being, and daily job satisfaction. Multilevel mixed-effects models and longitudinal mediation analyses will be used to examine lagged cross-domain spillover and PF as a within-person mediator. Discussion This study provides a fine-grained examination of how work and caregiving interact in daily life among employed family caregivers of people with dementia. By focusing on PF as a dynamic mediating mechanism, the study may identify actionable targets for tailored psychosocial interventions and workplace support strategies aimed at improving caregiver well-being and sustainable employment.
nbb1b2dd4d014: Rumba turning involves continuous whole-body reorientation, but discrete kinematic summaries do not localise where consistent directional deviations occur across the turn. This exploratory study examined rotational-progress-dependent patterns of pelvic obliquity, thoracic frontal-plane angle, and right support-foot progression angle during the initial 360° Rumba spiral turn in highly trained adolescent female Latin dancers. Fifteen dancers aged 14–16 years completed five valid trials each (75 trials). Three-dimensional kinematics were recorded using a 10-camera Vicon system at 100 Hz. For each trial, accumulated pelvic rotation was used to define rotational progress, and the three outcome waveforms were resampled to 101 points across 0%–100% of the turn. The five trials from each participant were averaged point by point, yielding 15 participant-level representative waveforms per outcome. Two-tailed one-sample statistical parametric mapping (SPM{t}) tests identified intervals in which group mean waveforms differed from their corresponding Plug-in Gait model-defined 0° references, using a Bonferroni-adjusted primary α = 0.0167 across the three outcomes. Pelvic obliquity showed a positive deviation at 11.3%–47.2% and a negative deviation at 56.5%–97.3% of rotational progress. Thoracic frontal-plane angle showed a negative deviation at 13.2%–41.9% and positive deviations at 57.6%–83.0% and 85.7%–92.0%. Right support-foot progression angle showed negative, positive, and negative deviations at 0.0%–4.8%, 10.4%–49.1%, and 56.2%–100.0%, respectively. Sensitivity analyses without the additional across-outcome Bonferroni adjustment preserved the principal directional patterns, with only modest changes in cluster extent and continuity. These findings identify where, across rotational progress, the measured segmental orientations consistently departed from model-defined references during a standardised Rumba spiral turn, without implying normative targets of optimal dance technique.
n8f57c2254dd3: by Sandra A. Allan, Emma N. I. Weeks The spectral sensitivity of adult Asian citrus psyllids, Diaphorina citri Kuwayama (Hemiptera: Liviidae), a vector of huanglongbing, was determined as a basis for optimization of visual traps. Electroretinogram responses were obtained from compound eyes of dark-adapted psyllids that were exposed to monochromatic 200 ms light flashes ranging from 340–700 nm. The spectral sensitivity curves were comprised of a peak in the ultraviolet region as well as a broad peak in the green-yellow region of the visual spectrum. Curves of male and female psyllids were similar and combined for further analysis. By fitting visual pigment templates to the curves, contributions from photopigments with maxima at 350, 430, 500, and 580 nm were revealed. In paired-choice attraction assays with sticky cards comparing colors at different intensities to grays of matching brightness, yellow and green were strongly attractive across the range of intensities, blue was generally repellent and red was not different than gray in attraction. By aligning specific photopigment sensitivities with behavioral preferences, this study establishes the physiological mechanisms underlying psyllid color attraction to guide the development of targeted visual monitoring tools.
nadcd13879708: Biophysical pleiotropy, the phenomenon in which a mutation affects multiple protein properties, underlies many genetic diseases and shapes protein evolution, yet remains poorly understood, limiting synthetic biology and therapeutic development. Although extensively studied in soluble proteins, little is known about how pleiotropic effects shaped the evolution of receptor protein functions. Here, we developed a cell-based assay designed to assess pleiotropic effects in G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs), the largest receptor class in eukaryotes. Because our assay allows for multiple GPCR molecular phenotypes (basal activity, ligand-dependent signaling, and cellular receptor abundance) to be simultaneously assessed, we applied it to study rhodopsin, a visual GPCR that evolved for high phototransduction capabilities by maximizing light-driven responses while minimizing noise. To investigate this, we integrated our assay with deep mutational scanning to test the impacts of ~2,000 single-residue substitutions in rhodopsin across all three molecular phenotypes (~6,000 measurements). By analyzing these data in the context of rhodopsin’s protein structures, we found complex pleiotropic effects that act asymmetrically to impose joint constraints, restricting mutational tolerance in rhodopsin’s retinal binding pocket and G protein interaction interface. A dose–response analysis of rhodopsin signaling revealed that these pleiotropic constraints arise from the dual functions of its chromophore, which acts as an agonist upon light-driven isomerization but also an inverse agonist in darkness. Because these constraints reflect mechanistically driven limitations in the evolution of receptor signaling, these findings reveal a role for biophysical pleiotropy in shaping the signaling capabilities of receptor proteins.
n3551b5ccd0bf: Nitrogen-fixing root nodules develop as lateral organs on legume roots and their formation is restricted by autoregulation of nodulation (AON), a systemic mechanism with unclear evolutionary origins. We identify Lotus japonicus NUCLEAR FACTOR Y subunit A4 ( NF-YA4 ) gene as a central target of the leucine-rich repeat receptor kinase HAR1, which controls both AON and root system architecture. Under nonsymbiotic conditions, HAR1 suppresses expression of NF-YA4 and its close paralog NF-YA1 , at least in part through a miR169-dependent mechanism, mirroring the Arabidopsis CLAVATA1/2-miR169- NF-YA module. Loss of HAR1 leads to NF-YA4 overexpression, broad transcriptional reprogramming, and induction of LATERAL ORGAN BOUNDARIES DOMAIN , STYLISH , and YUCCA auxin biosynthesis genes, enhancing auxin signaling and lateral root development. Grafting experiments show that HAR1 constrains NF-YA4 -mediated branching both locally in roots and systemically from shoots. Because NF-YA4 functions partly redundantly with NF-YA1 to mediate nodule emergence, our results suggest a model in which duplication and neofunctionalization of an ancestral NF-YA-dependent pathway controlling lateral root development facilitated its recruitment to the nodulation program. They also raise the possibility that AON could have evolved, at least in part, through the co-option of a LRR-RK/miR169/ NF-YA regulatory module that limited lateral root development.
n7616a17300ce: Constitutive modeling is fundamental to computational solid mechanics, yet most existing approaches remain material-specific and require retraining or recalibration when materials change. Here we introduce In-Context Modeling (ICM), a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling that infers constitutive behavior from physical context rather than material-specific optimization. Using hyperelasticity as a testbed, we demonstrate that ICM can be trained once on equilibrium deformation fields spanning diverse materials, geometries, and boundary conditions, enforcing physical equilibrium without stress labels. After training, the same model can be directly deployed on previously unseen hyperelastic materials without retraining. At inference, ICM treats a small set of nonuniform strain fields as physical context to generate constitutive response in a single forward pass. Numerical benchmarks and experimental validation demonstrate accurate stress prediction across out-of-distribution materials and boundary-value problems, together with substantial reductions in deployment cost compared with per-material learning approaches. These results establish in-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling, particularly valuable for heterogeneous biological tissues such as the brain, and suggest a pathway toward foundation models for computational mechanics.
nf0c6009ec030: Recently, we lost one of the original developers of the field of molecular electronics. Mark A. Ratner wrote a famous paper in 1974 that developed the theoretical framework for making a molecule act as a rectifier. This idea, and a host of further ideas that were stimulated by this and other papers, led to a huge amount of experimental and theoretical studies that continue to this day. But Mark’s career was much more than that, with leadership at Northwestern University and beyond that continues to shape the scientific enterprise.
n97527331ce2d: Allostery is central to catalysis and regulation, yet how distal perturbations control enzyme activity remains unresolved. Here we elucidate how a distal allosteric hot spot regulates catalysis in dihydrofolate reductase, a benchmark enzyme exhibiting latent allostery. We combine enhanced conformational sampling, reactive free-energy calculations of the chemical step, and perturbation-induced nonequilibrium molecular dynamics with evolutionary analysis and experimental kinetics to obtain a comprehensive molecular description of conformational landscapes, catalytic activity, and allosteric communication. We show that a mutational perturbation at the hot spot redistributes the populations of two globally similar conformations with a subtle but critical structural difference that makes one catalytically competent and the other not. Nonequilibrium relaxation simulations further reveal that the transition between these two states in the mutant proceeds through a stepwise sequence of local structural rearrangements rather than a concerted global motion. Guided by this mechanism, we rationally engineer a compensatory second-site mutation that partially restores activity. These results provide a unified thermodynamic and kinetic view of allostery and establish a general, mechanistically guided framework for engineering allosteric regulation in enzymes.
naf6a7c0d4c44: Macromolecular crowding is known to influence the diffusive, binding, kinetic, and equilibrium properties of proteins in a range of environments such as occur inside biological cells or in highly concentrated solutions of protein therapeutics. However a quantitative understanding of the effects of macromolecular crowding on the rates of protein-small molecule binding is lacking. Here, we present an adaptive model to simulate the association of two solutes in a macromolecularly crowded environment using Brownian dynamics and to compute the corresponding bimolecular association rate constant. The adaptive model represents interactions with atomistic detail for short-range crowder–noncrowder interactions, while using a coarse-grained approach for long-range crowder–noncrowder interactions and all crowder–crowder interactions. This multiscale approach is integrated in the Simulation of Diffusional Association (SDA) software for Brownian dynamics simulation of biomolecular diffusion. We applied this model to compute the rates of association for two contrasting protein-small molecule inhibitor complexes in environments varying in macromolecular crowder type and density, and we used Markov State modeling of the encounter trajectories to analyze the binding pathways. The results reveal competing effects: While the presence of the crowders can hinder ligand binding by reducing the translational diffusion rates of the solutes and obstructing the protein binding sites, crowders can also enhance the bimolecular association rate by other mechanisms, including channeling and the caging effect.
nb9a235fe18d5: Achieving reliable, remote control over multiple stable states in modular systems remains a challenge due to the coupling between modules and history-dependent transitions. Here, we present magnetic origami state machines that enable deterministic navigation from any unknown initial state to any target state under magnetic actuation. By assuming mutually distinct energy barriers in modular Kresling origami assemblies, we realize fully accessible transition graphs with scalable state spaces. Guided by the graph associated to the state machine, a rotating magnetic field induces a universal reset that autonomously drives the system to a known equilibrium state from arbitrary states without sensing or feedback, while pulsed magnetic inputs further enable programmable transitions to any target state via prescribed actuation sequences. A reduced-order Lagrangian mechanics model predicts snap-through dynamics across reset, stepwise programming (between graph nodes), and shortcuts (by adapting pulse magnitude and orientation) where inertia triggers simultaneous multicell transitions with a single pulse. These results establish a general framework for programmable magneto-mechanical state machines with autonomous state reset and full state-space control.
n18015d2920e0: UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGGT1) plays a central role in quality control of glycoprotein folding within the early secretory pathway, yet the molecular basis of UGGT1 substrate recognition remains poorly understood. Here, we report cryo-EM structures of human full-length multidomain UGGT1. Monomeric UGGT1 structures reveal two conformational states corresponding to “open” and “closed” architectures. Three-dimensional variability and molecular dynamics simulations suggest the existence of intermediate conformations, leading to a model in which a continuum of structural transitions underlies UGGT1 function. Notably, in the open state, the EM-maps reveal at the top of the U-shaped protein a density that bridges the sensory TRXL2 and the glucosyltransferase catalytic domains, consistent with substrate association. This observation supports a mode of binding that places the substrate near the catalytic domain. A dimeric form of UGGT1 was observed in which the glycoprotein substrate binding sites are occluded, suggesting that dimerization may regulate UGGT1 activity. To better understand the spatial relationship between the site of misfolding and that of UGGT-mediated N-glycan reglucosylation, we identified N-glycosylation sites on endogenous glycoprotein substrates by glycoproteomics. No consensus sequence was found flanking modified sites, indicating that substrate recognition relies on mechanisms beyond primary sequence. Mutations in the UGGT1 gene cause a novel congenital disorder of glycosylation characterized by developmental delay and intellectual disability, and the human UGGT1 structure helps explain how disease-associated missense and deletion variants disrupt function. Together, our data provide insight into the relationship between UGGT1 structure and function, integrating enzyme conformational states with client glycoprotein interaction and processing.
ne341b886c4e1: An opening salvo of lawsuits in US courts has begun holding AI companies accountable through independent doctrinal routes: Product liability and agency law cut as swords, while the shields of Section 230 immunity and First Amendment doctrine begin to crack. This Perspective points out that these converging paths share a unifying principle, built on the very engineering architecture of machine learning (ML) itself. Every ML system, across all variants, is constituted by a human-specified objective function before learning begins. Training data, deployment context, user interaction, and postdeployment oversight add further layers of deliberate human intention traceable to identifiable actors. AI output is therefore not the expression of a single speaker but a composite of layered human intents. It takes a village to raise an AI, and everyone in that village bears a duty of care. This transforms AI accountability from a philosophical puzzle into a tractable legal inquiry: Trace the chain of intentional design decisions across the ML pipeline, grade each actor’s responsibility by their intent’s specificity and foreseeability, and apportion liability accordingly, following the standard three doctrine-neutral questions (attribution, causation, apportionment). Sufficient for most cases, four gaps remain: who owes what share when many hands build one system, proving fault inside an opaque model, harms that surface only after deployment, and remedies that match the technology’s pace. Targeted reforms drawing on environmental, vaccine, and financial regulatory precedents can close these gaps without requiring new legal categories, AI speech rights, AI legal personhood, or defining AI consciousness.
n5ee98e94b56b: The activity of healthy neuronal networks is tightly regulated, and a shift toward hyperexcitability can cause various problems, such as epilepsies, memory deficits, and motor disorders. Numerous cellular, synaptic, and intrinsic mechanisms of hyperexcitability and compensatory mechanisms to restore healthy activity have been proposed. However, quantifying multiple compensatory mechanisms and their dependence on specific pathophysiological mechanisms has proven challenging, even in computational models. We use simulation-based inference to quantify the interactions of putative compensatory mechanisms in a spiking neuronal network model. Various parameters of the model can compensate for the changes in other parameters to maintain baseline activity, and we estimated their compensatory potential. Furthermore, specific causes of hyperexcitability – interneuron loss, excitatory recurrent synapses, and principal cell depolarization – have distinct compensatory mechanisms that can restore normal excitability. Our results show that spiking neuronal network simulators could generate hypotheses about the mechanisms of pathophysiological network mechanisms.
ncf001944f585: The microstructure of cells within the human cerebral cortex varies across the cortical ribbon, where changes in cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture are thought to endow each region of the cortex with its unique function. While fine-scale relative to a cell, these changes at the population level impact architectural properties of the cortex measurable in vivo by noninvasive MRI, such as the thickness and myelin content of the cortex. This raises the question of whether or not we can use these in vivo architectural measures to understand cortical organization, function, and development more broadly. Using the human visual cortex as a test bed, we demonstrated two architectural gradients, one in which cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture converge and another in which they diverge. These two gradients underlie the structural and functional topography of the visual cortex, even predicting the presence of new visual representations. Moreover, the two gradients show distinct visual behavior relevance and lifespan trajectory. These findings provide a more general framework for understanding the human cortex, showing that architectural gradients are a measurable fingerprint of functional organization and ontogenetic routines in the human brain.
n075e5562768b: In a previous study by our group (Nold et al., 2025), we investigated exercise-induced pain modulation after high-intensity compared to low-intensity exercise in a heterogeneous sample of diverse fitness levels. Exploratory analyses suggested an interaction of sex, fitness level, and drug treatment, indicating that males showed increasing hypoalgesia after high- compared to low-intensity exercise with increasing fitness levels, which was diminished when naloxone was administered. In contrast, these effects were not evident in females. These exploratory findings warranted further investigation to determine if and to what extent exercise-induced pain modulation depends on fitness level and/or sex. In this current study, we investigated an all-female sample (N=21) of high fitness levels using a similar paradigm as in the previous study, comparing heat and pressure pain ratings after high-intensity and low-intensity exercise. Our data show an interaction of exercise intensity and stimulus intensity in heat pain, with greater pain relief following high-intensity exercise, especially at the highest stimulus intensity. Despite results for pressure pain not reaching significance, a similar trend was evident. These results suggest that females at a high fitness level also show exercise-induced pain modulation for high-intensity compared to low-intensity exercise. Furthermore, we pooled the data of the current and previous study, providing evidence for fitness level but not sex to moderate exercise-induced pain modulation in heat pain. These findings suggest that exercise-induced pain modulation depends on fitness level but not on sex.
n58621760fa28: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) of larval Drosophila is widely used for studying synaptic transmission. Larval body wall muscles express five ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR) subunits that assemble into two tetrameric complexes, with subunit composition determining the strength and plasticity of synaptic transmission. Because NMJ function has been extensively characterized in larvae, it has commonly been assumed that adult fly NMJs share this molecular composition, despite substantial differences between life stages. Here, we systematically compare glutamate receptor expression across larval and adult Drosophila muscles. We find that adult leg and flight muscles exhibit different iGluR expression than larvae, lacking expression of several receptors previously considered essential. Adjacent muscles within the adult femur express distinct iGluRs, suggesting specialization of flexor and extensor muscles. Finally, the glutamate-gated chloride channel (GluClα) is expressed extrasynaptically in adult but not larval muscle fibers. Our results reveal unexpected heterogeneity in glutamate receptor expression across muscles and developmental stages, demonstrating the need for muscle-specific analyses in flies and other animals.
n34527b51d087: Core body temperature (Tb) is defended within narrow limits through thermoregulatory behaviors like huddling, nesting, and physical activity, as well as autonomic responses like brown fat thermogenesis. While Tb displays regulated fluctuations across different behavioral states and rest/arousal cycles, the neural control of these transitions remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the relationship between oxytocin neurons of the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVNOT) and behavioral and autonomic thermoeffector pathways across physiological states in mice. First, we show that PVNOT neurons are activated during social thermoregulation. We then demonstrate that in vivo PVNOT calcium dynamics align with transitions from rest to thermogenesis and behavioral arousal. Counter to our initial hypothesis, these dynamics were observed in both social and non-social contexts. Using a computer vision model to track thermoeffector pathways, we demonstrate that precisely timed stimulation of PVNOT neurons during low-Tb resting states increases thermogenesis followed by behavioral arousal. We therefore suggest a model in which PVNOT neurons facilitate homeostatic state-dependent transitions in thermo-behavioral states.
ne656e5f78819: The molecular mechanisms that drive (lymph-)angiogenesis are crucial to understanding diseases, such as lymphedema, that are caused due to malformations of the lymphatic vasculature. Recently, an interaction between the secreted protein Svep1, a key regulator in lymphangiogenesis, and the transmembrane receptor Tie1 was shown in zebrafish, humans, and mice. Here, guided by in silico AlphaFold-multimer structure predictions of SVEP1 complexes, we assert with protein binding studies that the human CCP20 domain is the primary binding site for TIE1. We further demonstrate that SVEP1 mediates strong binding of ANG2 and TIE1, and that combined stimulation of hdLECs with SVEP1 and ANG2 leads to phosphorylation of TIE1. TIE1 activation by SVEP1 and ANG2 enables downstream signaling and, in turn, potentiates nuclear exclusion of FOXO1 and phosphorylation of AKT compared to SVEP1 or ANG2 alone. We present a model in which ANG1/2 dimers bind to both SVEP1 and TIE1, resulting in the recruitment of multiple TIE1 receptor molecules to a multimeric complex at the cell membrane, potentially amplifying its signaling capacity.
n1ecafc6f9edc: Cross-condition bearing fault diagnosis often has to adapt to a new operating condition with only a few labelled target samples. This setting creates two coupled problems. First, the sparse target support set cannot describe the target fault distribution sufficiently. Second, the same fault class may occupy different feature regions across source and target conditions, which weakens source-domain pretrained classifiers. Existing methods usually improve few-shot learning or reduce domain shift, but they rarely enrich the labelled target-class representation before class-wise source-target alignment. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a target-domain augmentation and class-wise alignment framework for few-shot cross-condition bearing fault diagnosis. The rime optimization algorithm (RIME) is first used to optimize the variational mode decomposition (VMD) parameters K and α, and fault-sensitive components are selected using envelope entropy and adjacent modal-frequency overlap. The reconstructed signal is converted into symmetric dot pattern (SDP) images to provide a noise-suppressed polar representation. The fast generative adversarial network (FastGAN) then generates auxiliary target-domain SDP samples from the limited labelled target support set, making each target fault class less sparse. On this basis, class-wise maximum mean discrepancy (CMMD) is embedded into a Swin Transformer classifier to align source and target features within each known fault category. Experiments on the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) and Xi’an Jiaotong University–Shenyang Blower Works (XJTU-SY) datasets show that the proposed framework improves target-domain few-shot adaptation, achieving 93.33% and 97.58% accuracy under the G20 and G50 XJTU-SY target-augmentation settings, respectively.
nb27bc4136010: Photophobia encompasses a continuum of light-induced experiences from mild discomfort to overt pain and intolerance, yet clinical tools rarely quantify these distinctions, leaving many patients undiagnosed and untreated. This study employed the Ocular Photosensitivity Analyzer (OPA), a compact instrument for quantitative sensory testing (QST) with light, to investigate three perceptual levels in healthy adults: visual photosensitivity discomfort threshold (VPDT), visual photosensitivity pain threshold (VPPT), and an exploratory outcome, visual photosensitivity tolerance level (VPTol). Twenty-nine participants ages 19−34 underwent standardized OPA testing, during which they identified when light first became uncomfortable, painful, and intolerable. After each trial, participants rated the peak pain intensity (PI) and peak unpleasantness (UP) using visual analog scales. Measured illuminance values differed significantly across the perceptual levels (RM-ANOVA, N = 28, F(1.69, 45.6)=37.06, p ηp² = 0.58; Mauchly’s W = 0.82, p = 0.072), indicating sensory levels are differentiable. Post hoc t-tests revealed VPTol exceeded VPPT (N = 28, t(27)=−2.29, p = 0.030, dz = 0.43)), and both exceeded VPDT (VPTol: N = 29, t(28)=−7.69, p dz = 1.43, VPPT: N = 29, t(27)=−7.69, p dz = 1.47). Friedman’s test revealed UP (N = 28, χ2(2)=17.64, p Kendall’s W = 0.32) and PI (N = 28, χ2(2)=22.36, p Kendall’s W = 0.40) differences across perceptual levels and post hoc Wilcoxon tests showed UP and PI increased between VPDT and VPPT (UP: N = 29, Z = −4.34, p r = 0.57, PI: N = 29, Z = −4.58, p r = 0.60) and UP increased between VPDT and VPTol (N = 28, Z = −2.92, p = 0.007, r = 0.39), suggesting that both affective and sensory dimensions of pain vary across perceptual levels. Although preliminary, these findings are consistent with a multidimensional framework of photophobia. Additionally, the OPA’s ability to differentially quantify VPDT, VPPT, and VPTol offers a novel approach to characterize light sensitivity that may aid future assessment of abnormal light sensitivity.
n5873faec2ff1: by Christian Mesía-Montenegro Ceramic differentiation can involve altered associations among continuing attributes without wholesale categorical replacement. At Wacheqsa, Chavín de Huántar, Peru, this study compares ware composition, decorative techniques, and their associations in 1,308 decorated or surface-treated sherd observations from five archaeological contexts. Early Platforms and Water Flood constitute the earlier Urabarroid aggregate; Stone Rooms, Midden, and Late Platforms constitute the later Janabarroid aggregate. These labels describe ceramic affinities within pre-existing context sets, whose stratigraphic networks are only partly connected and whose formation histories differ. On identical common support of nine wares and six techniques (n = 334/822), ware-margin Hellinger distance is 0.430 (95% fixed-count interval 0.392–0.481), technique-margin distance is 0.588 (0.551–0.634), and joint distance is 0.734 (0.714–0.793). A homogeneous-association model rejects a common ware–technique association after aggregate-specific margins are fitted (G2 = 118.59; pboot = 0.0001); the result persists without Midden (G2 = 90.16; pboot = 0.0001). Early Platforms differs from each later context, and stamping/impression is prominent in all three later samples, although those contexts retain distinct joint profiles. Nine of eleven ware categories occur in both aggregates, with pronounced differences in the association of polished wares with incision and stamping/impression. The contrast is consistent with differing decorated repertoires across activity and depositional settings, including contexts associated with collective consumption. Local superpositions and the published chronology support a temporal interpretation, but the contribution of elapsed time cannot be separated from differences in activity and deposition.

n6bd441337296: With the deep integration of digitalization and artificial intelligence technologies into enterprise knowledge management, AI-assisted learning is reshaping the channels through which knowledge is acquired within organizations. Meanwhile, knowledge dissemination is evolving from traditional interpersonal interaction toward human-machine collaborative interaction. In light of this transformation, this study develops a multi-stage 2SEIR-CA dynamic model of knowledge dissemination under an AI-enabled mechanism that incorporates dual-channel “interpersonal–human-machine” interaction. Specifically, employees are classified into five states: employees who have not yet mastered the knowledge, employees with limited knowledge mastery, employees with strong knowledge mastery, knowledge-disseminating employees, and knowledge-exited employees. On this basis, the next-generation matrix method is employed to calculate the basic reproduction number of the system and to analyze the existence and stability of equilibrium points. An optimal control model is then established to derive strategies for promoting knowledge dissemination, and a cellular automaton model is introduced to characterize its spatiotemporal evolution. The results show that the system exhibits a pronounced threshold effect: when key dissemination parameters exceed their critical levels, knowledge can continue to diffuse within the organization; otherwise, it will gradually decay. Second, the AI-enabled mechanism enhances knowledge transformation efficiency and contact intensity, thereby significantly promoting the transition of employees with strong knowledge mastery to knowledge-disseminating employees. Third, the optimal control strategy proposed in this study can optimize transformation pathways across different stages under resource constraints, thereby improving overall dissemination efficiency and maintaining the structural stability of the dissemination system. Fourth, the spatiotemporal simulations demonstrate that, under optimal regulation, knowledge dissemination can form a stable diffusion pattern with high coverage. Under the assumptions and parameter settings of the proposed model, the findings provide theoretical insights into the dynamic mechanisms underlying AI-enabled knowledge dissemination and offer model-based implications for knowledge management practices in organizations.
n384e5e9b3dc8: Background Achieving early glycemic control in adolescents with diabetes is associated with improved short- and long-term health outcomes. The aim of this study was to examine the relationship between eating attitudes and glycemic control, as well as the factors associated with eating attitudes and glycemic control, in adolescents with diabetes. Methods This descriptive cross-sectional study included 143 adolescents with diabetes, aged 10–19 years, who attended a research hospital between February and April 2024. The data were collected using a Descriptive Information Form, Eating Attitudes Test (EAT) and an information form questioning the values of some metabolic variables. Results The mean age of the participants was 14 ± 2.3 years and 49.7% had diabetes between 1–5 years. The mean total score of the EAT scale was 16.62 ± 8.30. The mean score of the “Dieting” subscale of the EAT scale was 10.39 ± 5.58, the mean score of the “Bulimia food preoccupation” subscale was 2.33 ± 3.03 and the mean score of the “Oral Control” subscale was 3.79 ± 3.08. There was no significant difference between the mean EAT total score and glycemic control. Conclusions The mean EAT-26 total score was below the commonly used cutoff score, and no significant association was found between EAT-26 scores and HbA1c. Differences in EAT-26 total and subscale scores were observed according to selected demographic and clinical characteristics, including BMI, treatment modality, and treatment adherence. These findings describe self-reported eating attitudes in the study sample and support the inclusion of eating-related assessment within the holistic care of adolescents with Type 1 DM.
n2e971408be4f: Background Appropriate complementary feeding is essential for children’s growth and cognitive development. However, these practices remain inadequate in the study area. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the effect of nutrition counseling on complementary feeding practices among mothers with children aged 6–23 months in West Gojjam Zone, Northwest Ethiopia. Methods A two-arm, parallel, cluster-randomized controlled trial was conducted from June 2023 to December 2024 in rural districts of West Gojjam Zone. Thirty clusters (15 per arm) were assigned to either an intervention group (n = 401), which received Health Belief Model-based nutrition counseling by Women’s Development Army leaders, or to a control group (n = 401), which received routine education. The intervention was delivered monthly for nine months from infant age 6–8 months. The primary outcome was appropriate complementary feeding practices. Secondary outcomes included minimum dietary diversity, meal frequency, acceptable diet, and egg/flesh food consumption. Data were collected via interviewer-administered questionnaires. The intervention effect was analyzed using Generalized Estimating Equations with adjustment for potential confounders. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Results The difference-in-differences in appropriate complementary feeding practices between groups was 13.2 percentage points. After adjustment, mothers in the intervention group were nearly 2.5 times more likely to practice appropriate complementary feeding than controls [AOR = 2.49, 95% CI: (1.40, 4.42)]. Children of counseled mothers were also more likely to achieve minimum dietary diversity [AOR = 1.75, 95% CI: (1.04, 2.93)], minimum meal frequency [AOR = 1.62, 95% CI: (1.01, 2.61)], and minimum acceptable diet [AOR = 2.13, 95% CI: (1.26, 3.59)] compared with controls. Conclusion Health Belief Model-based nutrition counseling was positively associated with improvements in appropriate complementary feeding practices, minimum dietary diversity, meal frequency, and acceptable diet. Integrating such counseling into routine maternal and child health services may strengthen child nutrition programs in similar rural settings. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05871346).
n03c0fdbc30b2: Objective Enfortumab vedotin (EV) and cisplatin (CDDP) are central treatments for advanced urothelial carcinoma, yet the influence of prior CDDP exposure on subsequent EV efficacy remains unclear. In this report, we characterized EV-related drug responses in a CDDP-resistant bladder cancer subline. Methods A CDDP-resistant subline (HT1376-CR) was generated from parental bladder cancer cell (HT1376/P) through continuous exposure to CDDP. Sensitivities to CDDP, EV, and the EV payload monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE) were compared between HT1376-CR and HT1376/P. Nectin-4 expression, EV binding, and drug-resistance-related gene expression were evaluated. The effect of ABCB1 silencing on drug response was also examined. In vivo EV responses were explored using xenograft models. Results HT1376-CR cells showed increased sensitivity to EV in vitro and in vivo. HT1376-CR cells were more sensitive to MMAE and showed greater G2/M accumulation after MMAE exposure. In contrast, cell-surface nectin-4 expression and EV binding were reduced. ABCB1 was markedly upregulated in HT1376-CR, and ABCB1 silencing increased sensitivity to CDDP, MMAE, and EV within the resistant subline. Conclusion The CDDP-resistant HT1376 subline showed enhanced sensitivity to EV, and ABCB1 suppression further increased EV sensitivity within this resistant subline.
n0b8d90caeb55: by Gwangsu Lee Rising health insurance expenditure (HIE) poses fiscal risks and challenges to the sustainability of public insurance systems. Despite growing interest in data-driven analysis, empirical evidence on the associations between macroeconomic, social, and financial conditions and national HIE remains limited, particularly across provider types. This study introduces an explainable machine-learning framework with temporal predictive validation to analyze and forecast HIE using 60 macro-financial and socioeconomic indicators. The framework is applied to three monthly expenditure series from Korea’s National Health Insurance system (2000–2023). Predictive performance and interpretability are assessed using two univariate autoregressive baselines, three regularized linear indicator-based benchmarks, and six nonlinear indicator-based ensemble models. LightGBM serves as the primary explanatory model, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) quantifies indicator contributions and captures autoregressive persistence. Beyond associational insights, temporal predictive validation using lagged regression and Granger-type temporal predictive tests examines, within a prespecified exploratory lag window, whether SHAP-identified indicators show statistically supported exploratory lagged monitoring relevance. These results are interpreted as hypothesis-generating temporal monitoring evidence rather than as evidence of structural causal effects. Although persistence-based baselines achieved the strongest short-term forecasting accuracy, indicator-based models provided model-conditional explanatory information beyond autoregressive controls. The results indicate that shared macroeconomic pressures and provider-specific factors are associated with HIE predictions. The cost-of-living index is consistently associated with expenditure patterns across categories, whereas domestic demand and external conditions indicate provider-specific associations for medical institutions and pharmacies. Only a subset of predictors retained exploratory lagged monitoring support, underscoring the distinction between model-based predictive importance and hypothesis-generating monitoring signals. This integrated framework may inform transparent fiscal risk monitoring hypotheses and contextual review of public HIE.
n8a3f2aa8d192: Background Understanding factors influencing specialty choice is essential for workforce planning and curriculum development. Recruitment into diagnostic radiology remains challenging in several regions, particularly in low- and middle-income settings. This study aimed to identify factors associated with Palestinian medical students’ consideration of diagnostic radiology as a future specialty, with particular emphasis on educational exposure, perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI), and cognitive influences. Methods A multi-institutional cross-sectional study was conducted to evaluate factors influencing the choice of diagnostic radiology as a future specialty among Palestinian medical students between 2 November 2025 and 5 February 2026. Data were collected using a previously validated questionnaire adapted from Almuhanna et al. Descriptive statistics were performed, followed by bivariate analyses and multivariable logistic regression to identify independent predictors of considering radiology as a future specialty. Adjusted odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were reported. Results A total of 427 students participated (56.7% female; mean age 21.75 ± 2.1 years). Among 300 valid responses regarding radiology intention, 102 students (34.0%) reported considering radiology as a future specialty. In multivariable analysis, lack of exposure to radiology research (OR = 0.14, 95% CI 0.06–0.34, p < 0.001) and lack of preclinical radiology teaching (OR = 0.26, 95% CI 0.12–0.54, p < 0.001) were independently associated with a lower likelihood of considering radiology. Enjoyment of diagnostic problem-solving tasks (OR = 3.35, 95% CI 1.39–8.09, p = 0.007) and exposure to tele-radiology (OR = 3.96, 95% CI 1.72–9.12, p = 0.001) were independently associated with higher likelihood. Lifestyle, impact on patient care, and work environment were the most frequently reported motivating factors. Conclusions Palestinian medical students’ interest in radiology is strongly associated with modifiable educational exposures, cognitive engagement in diagnostic reasoning, and perceptions of evolving technological practice. These findings support the potential value of structured undergraduate radiology exposure, research opportunities, and mentorship initiatives to improve awareness and interest in radiology.
nd52a3225e818: This paper proposes a Meta-Transformer model for few-shot accurate lane-changing intention recognition in connected vehicle environment. Given the velocity, acceleration, distance headway, time headway and time to collision of a vehicle at past time steps, a transformer model is developed to recognize the lane changing intention of the vehicle at the current time step. The multi-head attention layer of the Transformer model is capable of effectively extracting features from the multivariate time serie input. This enhances the accuracy of lane-changing intention recognition. The Transformer model is combined with a model -agnostic meta-learning (MAML) algorithm to be able to perform well with small amount of training data. The meta-learning consists of meta-training and meta-testing. During the meta-training, a task is sampled from the distribution over tasks. The tasks include recognition of intention of lane-keeping, lane-changing to left lane, and lane-changing to right lane. The model is trained with few samples and feedback from the loss function defined on the tasks. The loss function is defined as the categorical cross entropy of the errors between the labels and the results generated by the proposed model. During the meta-testing, the model is tested on new data from the distribution of the transition from a feature and the label to another feature. The model is trained by minimizing the test error. Experimental results show that the proposed model can achieve 8.7 percentage points higher accuracy than a transformer model.
na345ebb4f393: Subgrade compaction is a critical procedure in highway construction. To elucidate the dynamic characteristics and energy transfer mechanisms throughout the entire compaction process, this study utilized four test lanes to conduct field experiments on highway subgrade under varying numbers of rolling passes. Comprehensive measurements and analyses were performed regarding the dynamic characteristics of vibration waves, energy distribution, and the evolution of soil compactness during operation. Furthermore, the compaction efficiency and energy transfer within the subgrade were quantitatively evaluated. The results indicate that the dynamic behavior of subgrade materials varies significantly across different compaction stages, which are consequently categorized into three distinct phases: loose, optimal compaction, and over-compaction. In this experiment, the third rolling pass represented the optimal compaction state, characterized by distinct resonance peaks, a regular frequency spectrum, and highly efficient energy transfer. As compactness increases, the horizontal propagation of vibration waves strengthens, whereas vertical attenuation accelerates, causing energy to concentrate beneath the vibration source. Additionally, the proposed method for evaluating compaction efficiency based on the energy transfer coefficient corroborates the three-stage evolution of the process, offering a direct, quantitative indicator for real-time quality assessment and endpoint determination. These findings provide new theoretical insights and empirical data to support intelligent and refined process control in subgrade compaction.
ncebda681b561: Dissecting the genetic basis of genotype × environment interaction (G × E) is important for breeding crops with stable or responsive performance across production environments. Using previously published seed-yield data from 107 Egyptian fenugreek accessions evaluated under two contrasting field environments, we investigated whether yield potential and environmental responsiveness share a common genetic basis. Seed yield per plant was measured in Giza (SYP_G; reference environment) and Wadi El-Natrun (SYP_W; contrasting environment). Nine derived indices were calculated to characterize environmental responsiveness, productivity, and stability: relative performance index (RPI), yield plasticity index (YPI), stress tolerance index (STI), log response ratio (LRR), mean productivity (MP), harmonic mean (HM), tolerance index (TOL), stress susceptibility index (SSI), and AMMI stability value (ASV). The near-zero correlation between SYP_G and SYP_W (r = 0.107) indicated substantial genotype reranking across environments, while several response indices were closely related to SYP_W and therefore predominantly reflected environment-dependent yield expression. Phenotypic analyses also identified contrasting performance strategies, ranging from highly responsive accessions, such as G15 (RPI = 3.629), to highly stable accessions, such as G41 (YPI = 0.001). These phenotypes were integrated with 38,142 SNPs using univariate association-mapping approaches. In addition, SYP_G and SYP_W were subjected to multivariate association-mapping. Association mapping identified one genome-wide-significant SNP for STI and several suggestive loci showed concordant associations across mapping methods. Within the current panel, marker coverage, and significance thresholds, most adaptation-index associations did not overlap previously reported yield loci; however, dDocent_Contig_39939_66, previously associated with seed yield in this panel, also showed cross-method suggestive associations with RPI and TOL. Comparative genomic analysis of three legume reference genomes supported two gene-linked candidate loci associated with STI: a cation/H⁺ antiporter and an importin subunit beta-1. The same analysis classified two of the strongest statistical signals, including the sole genome-wide-significant locus, as repetitive or transposable-element sequences rather than single-copy genes. These findings demonstrate that statistical association strength does not necessarily establish a coding-gene basis for loci identified using reference-free ddRAD markers. Within the current population size and marker coverage, environmental responsiveness and productivity appeared partially distinct but biologically connected components of environment-dependent yield performance.
